I want to propose a more explicit rule for test selection: certify exclusions using dependency proofs; include tests in unresolved dispatch, reflection, generated-code, and missing-dependency cones; and run the full suite if the uncertainty cannot be bounded. How should I express that?

Express it as a conservative selection policy. Exclude a test only when a dependency proof certifies that it cannot be affected by the change. If uncertainty from dispatch, reflection, generated code, or a missing dependency leaves a bounded set of tests potentially affected, include the tests in that unresolved cone. If the possible impact cannot be bounded sufficiently to make a safe partial selection, run the full suite.

This is a proposal for how to decide exclusions, not a claim that the required proofs or bounds have already been obtained.
What work is the word “certify” doing? Could an analyzer simply find no dependency and exclude the test?

“Certify” makes the burden of justification explicit. Finding no dependency in the information the analyzer happened to inspect is not enough if dispatch, reflection, generated code, or missing dependencies could conceal one. A dependency proof must support the conclusion that the test is unaffected despite the relevant possibilities. Without that support, the test remains a candidate for inclusion.
Does a dependency proof have to show that a test will pass?

No. It concerns whether the test can be affected by the change, not whether the test passes or fails. A test could fail for a reason unrelated to the change, and an affected test could pass. The proposed certificate supports an exclusion from change-impact selection; it is not a prediction of the test’s outcome.
What is an “unresolved cone” in this proposal?

It is the set of tests that must remain under consideration because an unresolved relationship could connect the change to them. The term is useful only if the cone conservatively contains every test that might be affected through that uncertainty. Calling a set a cone does not make an exclusion safe if a potentially affected test was left outside it.
If I can identify a bounded cone, am I allowed to run just the tests in it?

The proposal allows a partial selection when the uncertain impact can be safely bounded, but the selection must also include any other tests known or potentially affected through other relationships. Tests outside the cone may be excluded only where dependency proofs certify those exclusions. A bounded cone is not, by itself, a certificate that everything outside it is unaffected.
Does “unresolved” mean I have to resolve every possible dispatch target before selecting fewer than all tests?

Not necessarily. The proposal distinguishes resolving an uncertainty from bounding its possible effect. Even if a dispatch target remains unresolved, you may be able to identify a conservative cone of tests that could be affected and include all of them. If you cannot safely bound the possible effect, the proposal calls for the full suite. In neither case may you exclude a potentially affected test simply because the target is unknown.
Would a dispatch trace alone certify that a test outside an observed path is unaffected?

Not merely because the test does not appear in the trace. An observed path does not automatically rule out other possible dispatch targets. Any exclusion still needs a dependency proof that accounts for the unresolved possibilities. If those possibilities can be bounded, include the tests in their cone; if they cannot, use the full-suite fallback.
How does reflection fit the same policy?

A reflective relationship may leave possible impact invisible to ordinary call references. The proposal says to include tests in the unresolved reflection cone rather than interpret that invisibility as no dependency. Excluding tests beyond the cone requires a defensible bound and certified exclusions. If reflective impact cannot be bounded, run the full suite.
Should the proposal assume that identifying some reflective calls means the reflection cone is complete?

No. Identifying some calls can inform the analysis, but completeness is the relevant issue when excluding tests. A proposed cone must cover the tests that could be affected through the unresolved reflective relationships. If the available information cannot support that bound, the full-suite fallback applies.
What should happen when generated code creates an uncertain dependency?

Include tests in the unresolved generated-code cone. A dependency proof can justify excluding a test only if it accounts for the possible relationship involving generated code, rather than relying on what is visible in an incomplete source view. If the generated-code uncertainty cannot be bounded to a safe cone, run the full suite.
Would the presence of generated-source provenance automatically supply that proof?

No. Provenance can provide relevant information, but having it is not the same as certifying an exclusion. The proof must justify the particular conclusion that a test cannot be affected. Where the available generated-code information leaves a possible relationship unresolved, the tests in its cone remain selected—or, if the cone cannot be bounded, the full suite runs.
Missing dependencies seem harder: how can a cone be bounded when part of the dependency information is absent?

That is the question the proposed policy requires the analyzer to answer conservatively. Missing information might leave a possible impact that can still be bounded without excluding any potentially affected tests; if so, include the tests in that bound. If the missing dependency prevents a defensible bound, run the full suite. The proposal does not assume that a missing dependency is harmless or that its effect is always local.
Can I just define the missing-dependency cone as the tests whose known dependencies mention the missing item?

Not without establishing that this definition contains every test that could be affected. A missing dependency can be precisely the reason the known relationships are incomplete. The cone must be a safe bound on possible impact, not merely the tests for which a connection is already visible. If that bound cannot be justified, the fallback is the full suite.
Suppose a test belongs to more than one unresolved cone. Do I need separate selections for each type of uncertainty?

No separate run is implied. The selection must include the test if it belongs to any unresolved cone of potentially affected tests. The categories identify why it cannot safely be excluded; overlap does not make the test less relevant. The proposal does not prescribe how the analyzer represents overlapping cones internally.
What if I can bound a reflection cone but not a dispatch cone?

The unbounded uncertainty determines the conservative response: run the full suite. Bounding one source of possible impact does not justify excluding tests that may be affected through another source whose impact cannot be bounded. The full-suite fallback is for the case where a safe overall partial selection cannot be established.
Is “unbounded” meant to imply an infinite number of tests?

No. The full test suite is finite in any given run. Here, “unbounded” means the analyzer cannot establish a defensible narrower boundary on which tests might be affected. The full suite is then the safe selection because the analysis cannot justify leaving any potentially affected tests out.
So the fallback is not a way of pretending the dependency proof succeeded?

Correct. Running the full suite does not resolve the uncertain dependency or certify that any test is unaffected. It avoids making unsupported exclusions when the uncertainty cannot be safely bounded. The proof governs exclusions; the fallback handles the absence of a sufficient bound.
How do I prevent the proof requirement from becoming a formality—a certificate that merely says a test was not in the graph?

The certificate has to justify the exclusion against the relevant possible impact, including unresolved dispatch, reflection, generated-code, and missing-dependency relationships. If the graph might omit such a relationship, absence from the graph alone cannot prove the test unaffected. The proposal names dependency proofs precisely to avoid equating an incomplete view with a definitive negative conclusion; it does not prescribe a specific proof format.
Does this policy say every unresolved edge forces a full-suite run?

No. It says to include tests in unresolved cones when their possible impact can be bounded, and to run the full suite if it cannot. An unresolved relationship can therefore lead to a conservative partial selection, but only when its cone safely contains the potentially affected tests and exclusions outside it are certified. Uncertainty cannot be narrowed by assumption merely to avoid the fallback.
Could a large bounded cone push the selection above the 40% target?

Yes. A bound can be safe without being small. The proposal cannot drop tests from that cone simply to improve a percentage. The goal still calls for matching full-suite failure detection while selecting at most 40% of tests across 100 benchmark revisions, but this proposed policy does not itself establish that the numerical target is attainable. Its exclusions and fallback must remain sound even when a selection is large.
Does detecting every failure found by a full suite on a benchmark replace the need for exclusion proofs?

No. Failure detection on a benchmark compares observed outcomes; dependency proofs justify the exclusions the analyzer makes. A test may be potentially affected even if it does not fail in an observed run. The proposed rule is not to exclude it under unresolved impact merely because the benchmark happens to show no missed failure.
What would be a concise statement of the policy that keeps the bounded and unbounded cases distinct?

Certify each test exclusion with a dependency proof. Include all potentially affected tests within conservatively bounded unresolved dispatch, reflection, generated-code, or missing-dependency cones; if possible impact cannot be bounded safely, run the full suite.
And how should I describe its status relative to the test-reduction goal?

Describe it as a proposed safety rule for pursuing the goal, not as a measured improvement or a guarantee of a particular selection rate. It permits reduction where exclusions can be certified, preserves tests within unresolved but bounded impact cones, and chooses the full suite when no safe bound is available. Whether selections under that rule match full-suite failure detection while staying at or below 40% across 100 benchmark revisions is a separate outcome to establish.
Can dependency proofs bound MethodHandles and generated-source uncertainty cones without excluding affected tests or exceeding 40% mean test selection?

That remains an open question. A dependency proof would need to justify every exclusion despite possible impact through MethodHandles or generated source. If it can establish a conservative boundary around the uncertainty, tests inside that boundary remain selected; tests outside may be excluded only when the proof establishes that they cannot be affected. Whether those safe selections produce a mean at or below 40% requires measuring their sizes. Neither a sound bound nor a sufficiently small mean follows merely from proposing dependency proofs.
What does it mean to bound a MethodHandles uncertainty cone without resolving every target?

It means establishing which tests could possibly be affected by the unresolved targets, even though the targets themselves have not all been determined definitively. A safe cone contains every test that might be reached through those possibilities. The proof must also support excluding tests outside the cone; otherwise calling the cone bounded would hide a possible impact. If no defensible narrower boundary can be established, the proposed policy calls for the full suite.
Would instrumenting MethodHandles count as the dependency proof?

Not on its own. Instrumentation can supply information relevant to a proof, such as making an uncertain relationship visible. But visibility is different from a certified conclusion that particular tests cannot be affected. If the possible targets remain unresolved, the proof must account for that uncertainty rather than treating observed behavior as an exhaustive list without justification.
Could we simply include every test connected to a target seen in a MethodHandles trace?

Only if that selection conservatively covers all possible impact, including any relevant targets not established by the trace. The observed targets may help identify tests to include, but a trace alone does not necessarily establish that unobserved targets are impossible. The question is whether dependency proofs can justify the boundary, not whether an observed connection can be used as an optimistic cutoff.
Is a generated-source uncertainty cone defined the same way?

It follows the same safety principle: include every test that could be affected through the unresolved generated-source relationship, and certify exclusions outside the cone. The information needed to establish that boundary may differ from what is useful for MethodHandles. The question does not specify a proof construction for either category, so it would be premature to claim that the same evidence resolves both.
Would knowing where generated source came from be enough to exclude other tests?

Generated-source provenance can help explain a relationship, but provenance alone is not necessarily a proof that other tests are unaffected. The exclusion must be justified in light of all potentially relevant generated-code paths. If those paths remain uncertain, the affected cone must include the tests they could reach; if the impact cannot be bounded, the full-suite fallback applies.
What if a test could be affected through either MethodHandles or generated source?

It must be included if either unresolved cone could contain it. Establishing that it lies outside the MethodHandles cone would not justify exclusion if generated-source uncertainty still makes it potentially affected, and vice versa. A dependency proof for excluding the test needs to account for both possibilities.
Could the two cones overlap substantially without causing a problem for the proof?

Overlap is not a safety problem in itself. It simply means some tests have more than one possible route to impact. Count each selected test once when calculating a selection fraction, but do not treat overlap as evidence that either uncertainty has disappeared. The proof must still justify every exclusion outside the combined potentially affected set.
When I say “without excluding affected tests,” should I look only for tests that actually fail?

No. A test can be affected by a change without failing. The proposed safety rule concerns tests that could be affected, particularly where an unresolved relationship prevents a definitive analysis. Failure detection is an important outcome to compare with a full suite, but observing that an excluded test did not fail is not a dependency proof that it was unaffected.
Suppose a dependency proof covers one generated-source relationship but another remains unbounded. Could we still use a partial selection based on the first proof?

Not if the other unbounded relationship could affect tests outside that selection. A valid proof for one part of the analysis does not close a gap elsewhere. Under the proposed policy, if possible impact cannot be safely bounded overall, the full suite is the fallback. A partial selection would require a sound basis for all exclusions, not just some of them.
What would count as failing the safety part of this question?

Excluding a test that could be affected through an unresolved MethodHandles target or generated-source relationship would fail the safety condition, even if that exclusion made the selection fraction smaller. Likewise, labeling a cone bounded without establishing that it contains all potentially affected tests would not provide the required justification. The question asks for bounds that preserve affected tests, not merely for small-looking cones.
If the proof is conservative enough to select many tests, does that establish the first part even if the 40% mean is missed?

It could satisfy the non-exclusion condition while failing the efficiency condition. The two are separate: proofs must support safe exclusions, and the resulting selected-test fractions must be small enough for the mean not to exceed 40%. A conservative cone can be sound yet large. The numerical target cannot justify trimming that cone without proof.
Does staying under 40% mean selection establish that the cones were sound?

No. A low mean measures how many tests were selected, not whether those left out could have been affected. The proof obligation is what makes an exclusion defensible. Both soundness and the mean-selection threshold must be examined; one cannot stand in for the other.
If the full-suite fallback is used for an unbounded cone, does that count toward the 40% mean?

Yes. A full-suite fallback is a 100% selection for that run and belongs in any mean intended to describe the analyzer’s selections. The fallback protects against unsupported exclusions, but its frequency matters to whether the mean remains at or below 40%. This question provides neither the number of such fallbacks nor the other selection fractions.
Is it possible to answer the 40% part from the sizes of the MethodHandles and generated-source cones alone?

Not necessarily. The selected set may also include tests affected through relationships outside those cones, and a fallback can require the full suite when impact is unbounded. The 40% mean concerns the complete selected-test fraction on each evaluated revision, not just the sizes of two individual cones. Overlapping cones also should not be added as though the same test were selected twice.
How would you phrase the evidence needed to answer the question, without designing a new experiment?

You would need a justification for the boundaries of both types of uncertainty cone and for exclusions outside them, together with the resulting selected-test fractions from the revisions used to assess the 40% mean. The key checks are whether any potentially affected tests were excluded and whether the mean of the complete selections, including full-suite fallbacks, exceeds 40%. That states what an answer must establish without claiming that the evidence already exists.
Should the proof be allowed to treat a missing dependency as outside both cones and therefore irrelevant?

Not simply because it falls outside the two named categories. A missing dependency is another source of possible impact under the proposed selection policy. If it prevents a definitive exclusion and its possible effect can be bounded, its potentially affected tests must be included; if it cannot be bounded, the full suite is the fallback. The question focuses on MethodHandles and generated source, but that focus does not waive the safety condition for other unresolved relationships.
Can I conclude that bounding the two cones is impossible because MethodHandles and generated source can be dynamic?

No. Their uncertainty makes sound bounding a substantive question, not an impossibility established by the wording. Some uncertainty might admit a defensible boundary; other uncertainty might not. Without the needed proofs and selection measurements, neither feasibility nor infeasibility—and neither side of the 40% comparison—is established.
Give me a succinct formulation that keeps this as a question rather than a promised result.

Can dependency proofs conservatively bound the tests potentially affected through unresolved MethodHandles targets and generated-source relationships, justify every exclusion outside those cones, and keep the resulting mean test selection at or below 40%, with full-suite fallback where impact cannot be bounded?

Here is my hypothesis: proof-bounded uncertainty cones, with full-suite fallback for unbounded edges, will retain every affected test and average no more than 40% test selection on RevisionBench-100. Is that a precise answer to the question about safe bounds and selection size?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than an established result. It predicts two outcomes on RevisionBench-100: every affected test remains selected, and the mean selected-test fraction is at most 40%. Proof-bounded cones describe how the proposed approach would handle uncertainty when its possible impact can be safely bounded; full-suite fallback covers an edge whose possible impact cannot be bounded. Both parts matter to the prediction.
What does “proof-bounded” add to “uncertainty cone”?

It says the boundary must be justified by a dependency proof, not merely drawn around relationships that happen to be visible. A cone must contain every test that could be affected through the uncertainty it represents. Tests outside it can be excluded only if the proof supports that exclusion. Without a defensible boundary, the edge is unbounded for purposes of this hypothesis, and the full-suite fallback applies.
Does the hypothesis require resolving all MethodHandles targets before we can bound their cone?

No. A target can remain unresolved while a proof still establishes a safe bound on which tests it could affect. In that case, the potentially affected tests remain included in the cone. If the possible impact of the unresolved target cannot be bounded, the hypothesis calls for full-suite fallback instead. Neither case permits treating an unknown target as incapable of affecting a test.
And generated-source relationships fit the same hypothesis?

Yes. The question this hypothesis addresses includes MethodHandles and generated-source uncertainty. For either kind, a proof-bounded cone would have to include every potentially affected test and justify exclusions outside the boundary. If a relevant edge cannot be bounded safely, the full suite is selected. The hypothesis does not assert that either kind of uncertainty will always admit a small cone.
When I say it will “retain every affected test,” am I talking only about tests that fail?

No. A test can be affected without failing. “Retain every affected test” is a claim about the selection itself: no affected test is left out. Whether selected tests detect failures found by a full suite is a related comparison, but it is not a substitute for this stronger non-exclusion claim.
If a test outside a cone passes in a full-suite run, can we count that as proof it was unaffected?

No. Passing does not establish that the change could not affect the test. Under the hypothesis, an exclusion needs a dependency proof that accounts for the relevant uncertainty. The test outcome alone cannot certify that the cone’s boundary was sound.
Would observing no missed full-suite failures establish the “every affected test” part?

Not by itself. It would address observed failure detection, but an omitted affected test might pass. The hypothesis predicts retention of every affected test, so its safety part cannot be reduced to counting missed failures. The proof-bounded cones and the unbounded-edge fallback are meant to justify that retention even where a test’s outcome provides no warning.
What exactly happens when a cone is unbounded?

More precisely, when an edge’s possible impact cannot be bounded with a sound proof, the proposed approach selects the full suite. “Unbounded” does not mean the test suite is infinite; it means there is no justified narrower boundary for possible impact. Selecting all tests avoids excluding a potentially affected one merely because the dependency analysis cannot delimit the uncertainty.
Could we keep a partially bounded set and run only that set when another edge is unbounded?

Not under the unbounded-edge fallback stated in this hypothesis. A sound bound for one edge does not establish a bound for another. If the other edge’s possible impact cannot be bounded, selecting only the partial set could omit tests it might affect. The hypothesis uses the full suite for that situation.
Does a full-suite fallback count as retaining every affected test even though it does not prove which tests were affected?

Yes. Selecting the full suite retains every test, including every affected test, without requiring the analyzer to identify each affected one. The fallback does not resolve the uncertain edge or certify any exclusion; it avoids making exclusions while that uncertainty remains unbounded.
I also want the efficiency claim to be exact. Does “average ≤40% selection” mean that every RevisionBench-100 revision selects no more than 40%?

No. It predicts a mean selected-test fraction at or below 40% across RevisionBench-100, not a 40% ceiling for each revision. A full-suite fallback selects 100% on its revision and must be included in the average. Other revisions would need sufficiently smaller selections for the mean to stay within the hypothesized limit; the hypothesis does not give their individual rates.
So the fallback is compatible with the hypothesis, but not free in the average?

Exactly. Full-suite fallback is part of the predicted safety behavior, and each such revision contributes a 100% selection fraction. The hypothesis says that the complete pattern of selections, including those fallbacks, will nevertheless average no more than 40% on RevisionBench-100. It does not predict how many fallbacks will occur.
Does this hypothesis also say fallback will occur in at most five revisions?

No. Its numerical prediction is the mean selection of at most 40%. It specifies full-suite fallback for unbounded edges but gives no maximum count of fallback revisions. Adding a five-revision limit here would be an additional prediction, not something implied by this hypothesis.
Could the mean be at most 40% even if a proof-bounded cone is large on a particular revision?

Yes. A mean permits individual revisions above 40% if other revisions have smaller selections. The size of a cone on one revision does not determine the overall mean. But the approach cannot trim a large cone by excluding tests whose impact remains possible merely to reach the numerical target.
What if the cones retain every affected test but the mean ends up above 40%?

Then the safety prediction would hold on that assessment, but the efficiency prediction in this hypothesis would not. The hypothesis asserts both; meeting only one would not establish it as stated. The selection limit cannot override the requirement to retain affected tests.
And what if the mean is below 40% but even one affected test was excluded?

Then the safety prediction would fail, regardless of the low mean. This hypothesis does not allow an efficiency gain to compensate for excluding an affected test. Both retention and the mean-selection bound must hold.
How should I think about overlap between MethodHandles and generated-source cones when reading the mean?

A test that belongs to both potential-impact cones is still one selected test, not two. The mean concerns the fraction of distinct tests selected on each revision. Overlap may affect the size of the combined selection, but it does not relax either proof obligation: an exclusion must be justified against all relevant uncertainty.
Does the claim apply only to those two uncertainty types?

The motivating question focuses on MethodHandles and generated-source cones, but the hypothesis says *every affected test*. It cannot silently exclude tests that could be affected through another unresolved relationship. Proof-bounded selection must account for all relevant possible impact, and an edge that cannot be safely bounded invokes the stated full-suite fallback.
Can I say that dependency proofs will definitely be able to bound the cones tightly enough?

Not as an established fact. The hypothesis predicts that the proof-bounded approach will both retain every affected test and average at most 40% selection on RevisionBench-100. It does not supply proofs, cone sizes, or measured selection fractions. A bound can be sound yet too large to meet the predicted mean, and some edges may require full-suite fallback.
Does the 40% average by itself tell us whether exclusions were properly certified?

No. It measures selection size, not proof soundness. To satisfy the hypothesis, exclusions must have valid dependency justification, cones must contain the tests potentially affected through bounded uncertainty, and unbounded edges must trigger full-suite selection. Only then is the mean meaningful as an efficiency result achieved without sacrificing the stated safety condition.
How should the hypothesis be stated so it cannot be mistaken for an observed RevisionBench-100 outcome?

Use explicit predictive language: “We hypothesize that, on RevisionBench-100, proof-bounded uncertainty cones with full-suite fallback for unbounded edges will retain every affected test while averaging at most 40% test selection.” That preserves the safety and numerical predictions without claiming they have been demonstrated.

Let’s run the proof-bounded uncertainty cones on RevisionBench-100, audit excluded tests against the full suites, and measure mean selection and fallback frequency. How should I describe the activity?

Run the proof-bounded uncertainty-cone approach on RevisionBench-100. For each revision, examine the tests it excludes against the corresponding full suite, record the fraction of tests it selects, and record whether unbounded-edge uncertainty triggers full-suite fallback. Then measure mean selection and fallback frequency across the benchmark.

This describes an evaluation to perform, not its results. It does not yet establish whether every affected test was retained or whether mean selection is at most 40%.
Why audit excluded tests instead of looking only at the tests the cones include?

The safety claim turns on exclusions. A selected test cannot be omitted by that selection, but an excluded test could be affected if the purported dependency proof or cone boundary is unsound. Auditing exclusions against the corresponding full suites helps expose discrepancies, including tests that fail in a full-suite run but were left out of the reduced selection. The audit should also attend to whether the claimed proofs justify excluding those tests; a passing full-suite result alone does not show that an excluded test was unaffected.
Does the activity require running the full suite for comparison even when the proof-bounded selection is small?

Yes. The audit is against full suites on RevisionBench-100, so the corresponding full-suite results are the comparison for exclusions. That comparison run has a different role from the analyzer’s full-suite fallback: one supplies an evaluation baseline, while the other is the selection the approach makes when an edge cannot be bounded.
If the analyzer falls back on a revision, should I still include that revision when measuring mean selection?

Yes. A full-suite fallback selects 100% of the tests on that revision. Its selection fraction belongs in the mean across RevisionBench-100. Leaving fallback revisions out would understate the cost of the conservative behavior whose frequency the activity also measures.
What should fallback frequency count: unbounded edges or revisions where the full suite was selected?

For an across-revision fallback frequency, count revisions where an unbounded edge caused the approach to select the full suite. Multiple unbounded edges on one revision need not be counted as multiple fallback revisions. The activity does not prescribe a separate measure of how many unbounded edges occurred.
Can we use the fallback frequency alone to test the hypothesis about averaging no more than 40% selection?

No. Fallback revisions contribute 100% each, but selection fractions on revisions without fallback also determine the mean. Measuring both the mean selection and fallback frequency distinguishes the overall efficiency outcome from one reason it may become large. Neither measurement is supplied in advance by the activity.
What is the connection between a proof-bounded cone and an excluded test in the audit?

The cone conservatively contains tests that could be affected through the bounded uncertainty. To exclude a test outside it, the approach needs a dependency proof supporting that exclusion across the relevant possible relationships. The audit examines those exclusions against full-suite results and the claimed justification; simply observing that a test lies outside a proposed cone is not itself proof that it is unaffected.
Should a test in an unresolved cone be excluded if it passed in the full-suite comparison?

No. A passing result does not establish that the test could not be affected. If it remains in a conservatively bounded uncertainty cone, it stays selected under the proposed rule. The full-suite comparison can reveal observed failures, but it does not convert a potentially affected test into one whose exclusion is certified.
What if the full suite finds a failure in a test the approach excluded?

Record that discrepancy in the audit. It is direct evidence that the reduced selection omitted a test that failed under the full-suite run, and the exclusion’s claimed proof and cone boundary require scrutiny. The activity does not state that such a discrepancy occurs; it sets up the comparison needed to detect one.
And if no excluded test fails in the full-suite runs, does that establish the every-affected-test claim?

Not by itself. An affected test may pass, so an audit limited to observed failures cannot certify that every affected test was retained. The dependency proofs and conservative cone boundaries are essential to the safety claim. Full-suite results provide an important check on exclusions and failure detection, but absence of a missed failure is not equivalent to proof that all excluded tests were unaffected.
Could we call an exclusion certified just because the full suite passed that test?

No. Certification requires a dependency justification that rules out possible impact, including the relevant unresolved relationships. A pass is an outcome of a particular run, not a proof that the change cannot affect the test. Treating passing tests as automatically safe to omit would undermine the point of the exclusion audit.
If an edge cannot be bounded, how should the activity record the selection?

Under the approach being evaluated, an unbounded edge triggers full-suite fallback for that revision. Record that the analyzer selected the full suite, so its selected-test fraction is 100%, and include the revision in the fallback-frequency count. The comparison full suite remains the audit baseline; it should not itself be mistaken for a fallback.
Should the audit exclude fallback revisions because no tests are omitted there?

No. They still belong in the RevisionBench-100 evaluation and the mean-selection and fallback-frequency measurements. On a full-suite fallback revision there are no excluded tests to audit for that selection, but that is an observation about the selection, not a reason to remove the revision from the benchmark.
How do I calculate the mean without mistaking a pooled test count for a mean across revisions?

Calculate each revision’s selected-test fraction relative to its corresponding full suite, assigning 100% to a full-suite fallback. Average those fractions across RevisionBench-100. Pooling selected and available test counts across revisions is a different calculation if suite sizes differ; describe the calculation you use rather than conflating the two.
Is the 40% value a cap for every individual revision in this activity?

No. The hypothesis under examination predicts a mean selection of at most 40% on RevisionBench-100. An individual revision may select more, particularly if it falls back to the full suite. The activity measures the mean across revisions and separately records how frequently fallback occurs.
Would a mean below 40% make a missing proof acceptable?

No. The numerical result cannot justify excluding a potentially affected test without a valid proof. The activity evaluates both the safety side of the proof-bounded approach and its selection size. If a cone cannot safely bound an edge, full-suite fallback remains the appropriate selection even if that makes the mean larger.
Could the audit focus only on MethodHandles and generated-source uncertainty?

Those are important motivations for the proof-bounded approach, but the activity says to audit excluded tests against full suites on RevisionBench-100. An exclusion needs to be justified against any relevant possible impact; it would be unsound to ignore another unresolved path merely because the motivating question emphasized MethodHandles and generated source. The activity does not specify a category-by-category breakdown.
Does measuring fallback frequency tell us that every unbounded edge was correctly recognized?

No. It tells us how often the approach actually invoked full-suite fallback across the revisions. To support the safety claim, the audit must also consider whether purportedly bounded edges really have defensible bounds and whether exclusions are certified. A low fallback frequency alone could mean either effective bounding or overlooked uncertainty; the number does not distinguish them.
Can I say this activity has validated the hypothesis once the runs are requested?

No. Requesting or describing the runs establishes the evaluation activity, not its findings. The audit and measurements would need to be carried out before saying whether every affected test was retained or whether the mean is at most 40%. This node contains no observed selection fractions, fallback frequency, or audit outcome.
Give me a concise work instruction preserving the benchmark, the exclusion audit, and both measurements.

Run proof-bounded uncertainty cones on RevisionBench-100; audit excluded tests against the corresponding full suites, and measure mean selected-test fraction and the frequency of full-suite fallback for unbounded edges.

The RevisionBench-100 results for proof-bounded uncertainty cones are in: they selected 44% of tests on average, with zero missed failures. Generated-code fallbacks drove the excess. How should I report this?

Report the two measured outcomes separately: on RevisionBench-100, proof-bounded cones selected an average of 44% of tests and missed no failures found by the full-suite runs. The 44% mean exceeds the 40% selection target by four percentage points; generated-code fallbacks drove that excess. Zero missed failures is the observed detection result, not a reason to describe the selection target as met.
Does the 44% figure mean every revision selected more than 40%?

No. It is an average across RevisionBench-100. Individual revisions could have selected different fractions, including full-suite selections where fallback occurred. The result does not give the per-revision rates, so it cannot support a claim that every revision exceeded 40%.
And “four percentage points” is the right way to describe the gap?

Yes. The difference between 44% average selection and the 40% target is four percentage points. That describes the numerical excess without implying anything about how many tests or revisions produced it.
What does it mean that generated-code fallbacks drove the excess?

It attributes the above-target average to full-suite fallbacks associated with generated-code uncertainty. A fallback selects the full suite for its revision, which raises the average selection fraction. The finding does not state how many generated-code fallbacks occurred, how large the selections were on other revisions, or the precise generated-code relationships involved.
Can I say all full-suite fallbacks were caused by generated code?

No. “Generated-code fallbacks drove excess” identifies the source of the excess, but it does not say generated code caused every fallback. It also gives no fallback-frequency count. Keep the attribution to what is reported rather than turning it into an exhaustive breakdown.
Does “zero missed failures” mean no tests failed in the full suites?

No. It means the comparison found no failure in the full-suite runs that the proof-bounded selections missed. The result does not state how many failures the full suites found. An absence of *missed* failures is different from an absence of failures.
Could I say every affected test was retained because no failures were missed?

Not on that evidence alone. An affected test need not fail, so zero missed failures does not prove that every affected test was selected. The result reports failure detection against full suites; it does not give a separate finding that every excluded test was definitively unaffected or that every dependency proof was sound.
Then how should I distinguish what the result says about detection from what it says about safe exclusions?

For detection, it says the RevisionBench-100 comparison observed zero full-suite failures missed by the selected tests. For exclusions, the result supplies no conclusion that all potentially affected tests were retained. The proof-bounded policy calls for justified exclusions, but the absence of a detected miss is not itself a dependency proof.
Is it fair to call this a success because failure detection matched the full suites?

You can call the observed failure-detection outcome a match on RevisionBench-100. Calling the combined selection-and-detection objective met would be inaccurate: the average selection was 44%, above the 40% target. The two outcomes should remain distinct in the report.
Conversely, should I call the whole result a failure because it exceeded 40%?

You can say it did not meet the mean-selection target on RevisionBench-100. That does not erase the observed zero missed failures. A precise account states both: detection matched the full-suite results in the measured comparison, while average selection exceeded the target, with generated-code fallbacks driving the excess.
Do we know that the cones themselves were too large?

No. The stated attribution is to generated-code fallbacks. It does not identify large bounded cones as the cause of the 44% mean, nor does it quantify their sizes. Avoid assigning the excess to the cone boundaries when the reported finding points to fallback.
Does the result show that the generated-code fallbacks were unnecessary?

No. Their contribution to selection size does not establish that it would have been safe to omit them. Under the proposed policy, if generated-code impact cannot be bounded with a sound dependency proof, full-suite fallback protects against excluding potentially affected tests. The result gives no basis for declaring a narrower selection safe in those cases.
If eliminating those fallbacks would lower the average, can I recommend simply turning them off?

The reported excess is not permission to drop the conservative response to unresolved impact. Turning off fallback without a sound way to bound possible generated-code effects could exclude potentially affected tests. This result identifies where the measured selection excess came from; it does not establish a safe narrower alternative.
Could some generated-code relationships still have been handled with proof-bounded cones?

The result does not give a category-by-category account of which relationships were bounded. Saying generated-code fallbacks drove the excess does not mean every generated-code relationship led to fallback, or that none could be bounded. Those would be additional findings not present here.
Does 44% refer to a pooled fraction of every test available over all revisions?

The stated measure is an average fraction of tests selected on RevisionBench-100. Without an explicit pooled calculation and the relevant test counts, do not relabel it as a pooled fraction of all tests across all revisions. Calling it “44% of tests on average” preserves what was reported.
Were full-suite fallback revisions included in that average?

They are part of the reported average selection for the approach on RevisionBench-100. A fallback selects 100% of a revision’s tests; leaving such revisions out would not describe the overall selection rate or explain why generated-code fallbacks drove the excess. The result does not provide the individual fractions needed to reconstruct the 44% figure.
Can I infer a number of generated-code fallback revisions from the 44% mean?

No. The mean combines selection fractions across the benchmark. Without the rates on non-fallback revisions and the number of fallback revisions, there is no unique fallback count to infer from 44%. “Drove the excess” identifies a contributor, not its frequency.
Does zero missed failures show that the full-suite fallback had no value?

No. The observed detection match includes the selections actually made, including any full-suite fallbacks. You cannot infer what would have happened if those fallbacks had instead selected fewer tests. The result therefore cannot be used to say the fallback was dispensable.
Should I describe the 40% threshold as a per-revision cap here?
No. The comparison at issue is the mean selection on RevisionBench-100. The reported 44% exceeds that 40% mean target. This finding supplies no per-revision cap or per-revision selection outcomes.
What can I say about the role of missing dependencies, reflection, and MethodHandles in this result?

The result does not break down their effects. It reports an overall 44% average, zero missed failures, and generated-code fallbacks as the driver of the excess. It would be unwarranted to attribute a particular selection fraction, fallback, or detection outcome to missing dependencies, reflection, or MethodHandles from this summary.
Does the result tell us that the dependency proofs were valid?

No. It reports selection and observed failure detection, with an attribution for the selection excess. Zero missed failures is consistent with the selected tests finding everything the full suites found on these revisions, but it does not independently certify every exclusion proof or show that no affected passing test was omitted.
I want one final sentence that preserves the efficiency miss, the observed detection result, and the stated cause without overclaiming safety.

On RevisionBench-100, proof-bounded uncertainty cones selected 44% of tests on average—four percentage points above the 40% target—with generated-code fallbacks driving the excess; the comparison with full-suite runs found zero missed failures.

I propose extending proof-bounded uncertainty cones with hermetic generator-input fingerprints and generated-source provenance. If the generator inputs or provenance are unresolved, use the full suite. How should I describe this proposal?

Describe it as an extension of the proof-bounded selection policy. Use hermetic generator-input fingerprints and generated-source provenance as information for reasoning about dependencies involving generated code. Continue to certify exclusions through dependency proofs and retain tests within any conservatively bounded uncertainty cones. If the generator inputs or the provenance remain unresolved, select the full suite instead of excluding potentially affected tests.

This states a proposed design, not a claim that the fingerprints or provenance have already resolved any particular case.
What does the generator-input fingerprint contribute to an exclusion proof?

It is intended to give the analysis a basis for reasoning about the inputs relevant to generated source. A proof of non-impact must account for possible generated-code relationships rather than assume they do not exist. A trustworthy, hermetic fingerprint could contribute information about those inputs, but the presence of a fingerprint is not itself a proof that a particular test is unaffected.
Why specify that the fingerprints are hermetic?

The word signals that the fingerprint should reflect the generator inputs on which the relevant reasoning depends, rather than quietly omitting influences that could change the generated source. If the supposed input view leaves a relevant input unresolved, it cannot justify a definitive exclusion. The proposal does not prescribe how hermeticity is implemented or establish that it has been achieved.
Can I interpret hermeticity as a guarantee that any matching fingerprint means the generated output must be identical?

Do not assume that guarantee from the proposal alone. A matching fingerprint would be useful for dependency reasoning only if it covers the relevant inputs and the reasoning connecting inputs to generated source is justified. This proposal names hermetic generator-input fingerprints as a component; it does not specify a fingerprinting method or prove that equality of fingerprints certifies every property of generated output.
Does generated-source provenance answer the same question as the input fingerprint?

No. The fingerprint concerns the inputs to generation, while provenance concerns where generated source came from and how it relates to its origins. Both can inform a dependency proof involving generated code. Neither should silently stand in for the other: if provenance is unresolved, knowing something about inputs does not remove the proposed full-suite fallback, and unresolved inputs are not made safe merely by having provenance.
So if I have a fingerprint but cannot establish provenance for the generated source, can I still make a reduced selection?

Not under the fallback condition as stated. If provenance is unresolved, the proposal calls for the full suite. The fingerprint cannot substitute for the missing provenance in an exclusion argument that depends on a generated-source relationship.
And what if provenance is available but some generator input cannot be accounted for?

That also calls for the full suite under this proposal: unresolved inputs trigger the fallback. Provenance may explain a known origin, but it does not certify that an unaccounted-for input cannot change generated source or affect tests. The two sources of information have to support the exclusion argument together where both are relevant.
Does “inputs or provenance are unresolved” mean I need both unresolved before the fallback applies?

No. “Or” means either condition is sufficient. If inputs are unresolved, use the full suite; if provenance is unresolved, use the full suite. The fallback also applies if both remain unresolved. Do not reinterpret the condition as requiring both kinds of uncertainty simultaneously.
Could I bound a small cone around a generated file and use that instead when the generator inputs are unresolved?

The proposed rule here explicitly says to use full suites when inputs or provenance are unresolved. A small-looking cone does not replace that fallback merely because it would be more efficient. Proof-bounded cones remain useful where the information needed for safe bounds is available, but unresolved generator inputs or provenance invoke the full-suite condition in this proposal.
Would it be fair to say the proposal lets a fingerprint automatically exclude every test outside the generated-source cone?

No. Exclusions still require dependency proofs. A fingerprint can inform a proof about generated-code dependencies, but it does not independently establish that every test outside a proposed cone is unaffected. The cone has to conservatively cover possible impact, and each exclusion must be justified against the relevant relationships.
What if the fingerprints and provenance are both available but the proof still cannot bound a relevant dependency?

Availability of those two pieces of information does not guarantee that an impact relationship is resolved. Under the proof-bounded-cone policy, if possible impact cannot be bounded safely, the conservative response is the full suite. This extension adds information and states an explicit fallback for unresolved inputs or provenance; it does not turn incomplete dependency proofs into valid exclusions.
I want to avoid suggesting that generated-source provenance means generated code itself has already been analyzed completely.

That restraint is appropriate. Provenance provides information about origin, not automatic completeness of change-impact analysis. It may help support a proof, but a proof still needs to establish which tests could be affected. When provenance is unresolved, the proposal specifically chooses a full-suite run.
Does the proposal tell us which generator inputs are included in a fingerprint, or how it is computed?

No. It names hermetic generator-input fingerprints but does not specify their construction, representation, or a list of inputs. You can state the information they are meant to contribute without inventing a computation procedure or claiming that all necessary inputs have been captured.
What exactly must a dependency proof justify after this extension?

It must justify excluding the particular test despite any relevant possible impact, including relationships involving generated source and its inputs. A fingerprint or provenance record can be part of that justification, but neither is a blanket exemption from considering other possible dependencies. If the necessary generator inputs or provenance remain unresolved, the proposed selection is the full suite rather than a proof-based exclusion.
Does this change how unresolved dispatch or reflection should be treated?

The extension does not waive the conservative handling of other uncertainty. Proof-bounded cones still have to account for unresolved dispatch and reflection when assessing possible impact, with full-suite selection where a safe bound cannot be established. The new explicit condition concerns unresolved generator inputs or generated-source provenance; it should not be read as permission to exclude tests affected through another unresolved route.
Could a test be excluded merely because the generated-source fingerprint did not change?

Not merely for that reason. Exclusion needs a dependency proof establishing that the test cannot be affected by the change, taking account of the generated-source relationship and other relevant paths. An unchanged fingerprint is potentially useful information only insofar as its scope and connection to the impact claim are justified. If inputs or provenance are unresolved, the full-suite fallback applies.
Is the full-suite path a way of declaring that provenance does not matter?

No. It acknowledges that unresolved provenance matters enough to prevent a safe narrower exclusion. Running the full suite preserves potentially affected tests without claiming that their generated-source dependencies have been definitively analyzed. The fallback is a response to uncertainty, not a resolution of it.
Can I say this extension will definitely keep selection under the 40% target?

No. The proposal aims to make some generated-code dependency reasoning more informative while preserving conservative full-suite behavior when inputs or provenance cannot be resolved. It provides no measured selection rates or fallback frequency. Whether it can meet the goal of selecting at most 40% of tests across 100 benchmark revisions while matching full-suite failure detection remains to be established.
Could frequent full-suite runs be hidden by reporting selection rates only where fingerprints and provenance are available?

That would not describe the proposed analyzer’s overall selection. Revisions where unresolved inputs or provenance trigger a full-suite run select 100% of the tests and must count in any assessment of its test-selection rate. Restricting the calculation to cases permitting reduced selection would conceal the cost of the fallback.
Would a full-suite comparison showing no missed failures prove that the fingerprints are hermetic?

No. Failure detection on a benchmark is an observed comparison, not proof that a fingerprint accounts for every relevant generator input. The dependency proofs need a sound basis, and unresolved inputs or provenance invoke the fallback regardless of whether observed runs happen to show missed failures.
If a generated source has several possible origins and one remains unresolved, should I act as if only the known origins matter?

No. An unresolved possible origin means provenance is not definitive for the relevant exclusion claim. Under this proposal, unresolved provenance leads to a full-suite run. Considering only known origins and dropping the unresolved possibility would turn missing information into an unjustified claim that tests are unaffected.
Would it be accurate to describe fingerprints and provenance as ways to reduce fallback rather than as reasons to weaken it?

Yes, as an intended role rather than an observed outcome. They may provide information that supports sound dependency proofs and bounded selections when inputs and provenance are resolved. But the proposal retains the full suite when either remains unresolved; it does not authorize a narrower selection simply to avoid fallback. No reduction in fallback frequency is established by proposing the extension.
Please give me a compact wording that keeps the proof requirement, both new sources of information, and the exact fallback condition.

Extend proof-bounded uncertainty cones with hermetic generator-input fingerprints and generated-source provenance to support dependency proofs for exclusions; run the full suite whenever the generator inputs or the provenance are unresolved.

Let’s rerun RevisionBench-100 with generator-input fingerprints and provenance manifests. I want to audit fallback triggers, excluded tests, mean test selection, and failures found by the full suites. How should I describe this activity?

Rerun RevisionBench-100 with generator-input fingerprints and provenance manifests available to the proof-bounded analysis. That is not what it says. The stated fallback condition is *unresolved inputs*. Generator inputs that can be accounted for do not, merely by existing, invoke this fallback. Nor should a smaller selection be assumed safe solely because an input has a fingerprint or a trace.
