They have different roles. A completeness check assesses whether trace information can support the reasoning being attempted. Full-suite fallback is the selection response when relevant input uncertainty remains unresolved. The patch includes both; it does not equate the existence of a trace with resolution of every input.
Suppose the trace passes its completeness check, but a relevant generator input is still unresolved. Can the fallback be skipped?

Not on the strength of trace completeness alone. A complete trace may support a particular conclusion about generator activity, but it does not automatically settle every input relationship. If an input remains unresolved for the impact decision, the stated fallback is the full suite.
And if a fingerprint is available but the trace needed to justify non-use is incomplete?

The fingerprint cannot make an unsupported non-use claim valid. If that missing trace information leaves a relevant input unresolved, select the full suite. The patch’s components complement each other; the presence of one does not erase uncertainty exposed by another.
Should I say the patch guarantees complete sandbox traces?

No. It adds *completeness checks*, not a guarantee that every sandbox trace is complete. That distinction matters because a check may leave the analysis unable to rely on a trace. The unresolved-input fallback remains part of the patch for cases where a definitive selection cannot be supported.
Does the patch specify the realpath resolution method or the exact trace-check algorithm?

No. The artifact names realpath generator fingerprints and sandbox trace completeness checks, but gives no algorithm, data format, or detailed checking procedure. Describing those as specified implementation choices would add facts beyond the patch’s stated contents.
Could I say this patch fixes every uncertainty involving generated code?

That would be too broad. It adds information and checks relevant to generator inputs, along with a conservative response when inputs remain unresolved. Its explicit fallback anticipates that not every input question will be settled. It does not claim to resolve every generated-code dependency or certify every test exclusion.
What if another dependency question remains unresolved even though the generator inputs are clear?

Clear generator-input information would not settle a different possible impact relationship. This artifact specifically identifies full-suite fallback for unresolved inputs; it should not be described as resolving other uncertainty by implication. Any test exclusion must still have an adequate basis rather than relying on the absence of an input problem.
Does the existence of the CI patch tell us what mean percentage of tests CI selects?

No. The patch description lists its components, not measured CI selection rates. Full-suite fallback can affect selection when invoked, but this artifact supplies no frequency or average from which to calculate a percentage.
Does it establish that CI detected every failure found by a full suite?

No new failure-detection comparison is stated for this artifact. The patch includes safeguards intended to prevent unsafe exclusions when inputs remain unresolved, but its contents alone are not a measured failure-detection result.
How should I distinguish a full-suite run made for comparison from the fallback in this patch?

A comparison run supplies a baseline for evaluating detection. The patch’s fallback is CI selecting the full suite because relevant input information remains unresolved. Only the latter describes the selection behavior added by the patch; a baseline run does not by itself show that fallback was invoked.
Can I call full-suite fallback an exception we are free to disable if it raises the selection rate?

No. It is an explicit part of the patch’s conservative handling of unresolved inputs. Disabling it simply to reduce the number of tests run would leave a gap in the stated behavior and could permit exclusion of potentially affected tests without a definitive analysis.
Please give me a short description of the deliverable that separates its analysis components from its CI response.

The TraceGuard CI patch adds realpath generator fingerprints and sandbox trace completeness checks for impact analysis, together with full-suite fallback whenever relevant generator inputs remain unresolved.

I’d like to propose SoundSlice: classloader-backed per-test reachability certificates with dispatch closure. If reflection, generators, or missing dependencies remain unresolved, it runs the full suite. How should I describe the approach?

Describe SoundSlice as a proposed change-impact test selector that justifies exclusions test by test. Its classloader-backed reachability certificates would establish when a particular test cannot be affected by a change, with dispatch closure accounting for possible dynamic targets. If reflection, generators, or missing dependencies leave relevant impact unresolved, SoundSlice selects the full suite instead of excluding potentially affected tests. That is the proposed behavior, not a claim that the certificates have already been built or validated.
Why make the certificates per-test rather than issuing one statement about the entire suite?

A per-test certificate ties an exclusion to the particular test being omitted. SoundSlice could select tests whose impact cannot be ruled out while excluding a different test only if its certificate supports that decision. A general statement that the analyzer found no impact would be less precise about which exclusions are justified. The proposal does not specify a certificate format or guarantee that every test can receive one.
Does a reachability certificate say that a test will pass?

No. It concerns whether the changed behavior could be reached by that test under the relationships the certificate must account for. It is not a prediction of the test’s pass or fail result. A passing test might still be affected, so SoundSlice cannot substitute a passing observation for a sound certificate of non-impact.
What does “classloader-backed” contribute? I don’t want to imply a detailed implementation that I haven’t specified.

It identifies classloader information as part of the basis for SoundSlice’s per-test reachability certificates. That matters when reasoning about what code a test might reach, but the proposal does not prescribe how classloader activity is captured, represented, or checked. You can name the classloader-backed basis without claiming that classloader information alone settles reflection, generated-code behavior, or missing dependencies.
Could I simply say that the classloader tells us everything a test can reach?

That would be too strong. The proposal combines classloader-backed certificates with dispatch closure and retains full-suite fallback for unresolved reflection, generators, or missing dependencies. Those qualifications would be unnecessary if classloader information automatically supplied a complete account of every possible impact. A certificate must justify its reachability conclusion rather than assume completeness merely because classloader information is available.
What does dispatch closure mean in the certificate’s reasoning?

It means the reachability reasoning must account for the possible targets of dynamic dispatch, rather than treating one apparent target as the only one. An exclusion is sound only if its certificate rules out impact across the dispatch possibilities relevant to that test. The proposal names dispatch closure but does not specify an algorithm for calculating it or claim that every possible target will always be resolved.
If a trace shows just one dispatch target, may the certificate rule out every other target?

Not solely because the other targets were not observed. A trace can provide useful information, but dispatch closure needs a defensible basis for accounting for relevant possible targets. Otherwise a certificate could exclude a test based on an incomplete view of dynamic dispatch. SoundSlice’s proposed certificate cannot turn an unobserved possibility into an impossible one without justification.
Does SoundSlice require a certificate for a test it selects?

The proposed certificate is the basis for excluding a test. Selecting a test does not require proving it is affected; it may be selected precisely because possible impact has not been ruled out. The important asymmetry is that uncertainty can justify inclusion, while exclusion needs a supported non-impact conclusion.
Suppose one test has a convincing certificate but another test does not. Does that force both to run?

The per-test aspect allows their exclusion decisions to be considered separately where the relevant analysis is definitive. But the proposal also states a full-suite fallback when reflection, generators, or missing dependencies remain unresolved. If one of those unresolved conditions applies to the selection at hand, do not override the specified fallback merely because another test has a certificate. The proposal does not spell out a finer-grained exception to that full-suite rule.
So I shouldn’t quietly replace the full-suite fallback with a cone of apparently related tests?

Correct. SoundSlice, as proposed here, uses the full suite when the named uncertainty remains unresolved. Selecting only an apparently related subset would be a different fallback and would require its own justification. The certificates can support individual exclusions when their reachability claims are sound, but they cannot be used to wish away an unresolved condition that triggers the stated full-suite response.
Why are reflection and generators both explicit fallback conditions?

Either can leave a relationship between a change and a test unclear. Reflective behavior may not be captured by an ordinary apparent call path; generated code can introduce relationships that are not established by an incomplete view of its inputs and output. SoundSlice’s proposal does not assume its reachability certificates resolve these cases automatically. If reflection or generators remain unresolved, it chooses the full suite rather than make unsupported exclusions.
When the proposal says “unresolved generators,” does that mean every use of generated code requires a full-suite run?

No. The condition is unresolved generator-related impact, not the mere presence of generated code. Where the relevant relationship can be accounted for definitively, generated code alone does not state a reason to invoke fallback. Where it remains unresolved, the proposal says to run the full suite.
Does the same distinction apply to reflection?

Yes. The proposal does not say every reflective call automatically forces the full suite. It says unresolved reflection does. The analyzer must not describe a reflective relationship as resolved merely because a partial observation makes it seem unlikely to matter.
And why is a missing dependency a fallback condition instead of something we can ignore until it is available?

A missing dependency may be exactly what prevents a reachability certificate from ruling out possible impact. Its absence from the information SoundSlice can inspect is not evidence that no test can reach relevant behavior through it. Under the proposal, unresolved impact due to a missing dependency triggers the full suite rather than an exclusion based on that gap.
If a certificate says a test is unreachable from the change but depends on information from a missing dependency, is it still a valid certificate?

It cannot be treated as definitive if the missing dependency could change that reachability conclusion. The certificate must support the non-impact claim despite the relevant possibilities. If the dependency remains missing and prevents that determination, SoundSlice’s proposed response is full-suite fallback, not acceptance of a certificate whose crucial premise is unknown.
What if the classloader-backed information shows an observed path to a changed component?

Then that observation cannot support a claim that the path is absent. More generally, information about a possible route to impact is a reason to keep the test under consideration unless a sound analysis rules that route out. The proposal does not say that every observed path necessarily causes a test failure; reachability and failure are different questions.
How should a certificate handle another possible path it has not analyzed?

It must not certify exclusion as though that path were ruled out. A per-test reachability certificate has to cover the relevant possibilities, including dispatch closure and any reflective or generated-code relationships that could affect the test. If a named source of impact remains unresolved, the full-suite fallback applies. An incomplete certificate is not a definitive negative conclusion.
Would matching the full suite’s failures in an evaluation be enough to validate every certificate?

No. A test can be affected without failing in a particular run. Matching observed full-suite failure detection would address an important evaluation requirement, but it would not, by itself, demonstrate that every excluded test had a sound reachability certificate. SoundSlice still needs its certificates and conservative fallback to justify exclusions under uncertainty.
The design goal also asks for at most 40% of tests across 100 benchmark revisions while matching full-suite failure detection. Does this proposal claim it can do that?

It does not report that outcome. SoundSlice offers a proposed way to seek safe reductions: certify exclusions per test, account for dispatch possibilities, and use the full suite when the specified uncertainties remain unresolved. Full-suite fallbacks could make the selection target difficult to meet, so both the selection percentage across the 100 revisions and detection relative to their full suites would need to be assessed. The proposal itself supplies no measurements.
Could SoundSlice skip a needed fallback to keep the selection rate under 40%?

No. The numerical target cannot justify excluding potentially affected tests when reflection, generators, or missing dependencies prevent a definitive analysis. If such uncertainty remains unresolved, SoundSlice’s stated response is the full suite, even if that makes the percentage target harder to achieve. Efficiency must be attained through justified exclusions, not by relaxing the safety condition.
Does a full-suite fallback certify that all the tests were affected?

No. It selects every test because SoundSlice cannot safely rule out the relevant possibilities. It need not identify which tests truly are affected, and it does not resolve the underlying uncertainty. Its purpose is to avoid unsupported exclusions.
Is there a concise way to distinguish the two possible outcomes for a test without inventing an implementation workflow?

You can say that a test is excluded only when a classloader-backed, dispatch-closed per-test reachability certificate justifies exclusion. Otherwise, it remains selected as appropriate to the impact analysis; if reflection, generators, or missing dependencies remain unresolved, SoundSlice runs the full suite. That states the proposal’s decision principles without prescribing how certificates are stored or generated.
Would it overstate things to call SoundSlice a proved-safe replacement for full-suite regression testing?

Yes. SoundSlice is a proposal for an analyzer with proof-based exclusions and a conservative full-suite fallback. Its name and intended certificate structure do not establish that certificates are sound in every case or that it achieves the benchmark selection and detection targets. Where the named uncertainty remains unresolved, it deliberately does not replace the full suite.
Please give me a compact proposal statement that retains the name, certificate basis, dispatch closure, and all three fallback categories.

Use SoundSlice to justify test exclusions with classloader-backed per-test reachability certificates that account for dispatch closure; run the full suite whenever reflection, generators, or missing dependencies leave relevant impact unresolved.
Can SoundSlice invalidate per-test certificates when classloaders dynamically introduce implementations, without exceeding 40% mean test selection on RevisionBench-100?

That is an open question with two parts. SoundSlice would need to recognize when a newly introduced implementation changes the possible dispatch targets on which a per-test reachability certificate depends, and stop using any certificate whose non-impact conclusion is no longer justified. It would also need to keep mean test selection on RevisionBench-100 at or below 40% after accounting for any tests that must be retained. The proposal supplies neither a demonstrated invalidation mechanism nor a measured selection result.
Why might an implementation introduced through a classloader affect a certificate for one test?

A certificate excluding a test relies on its account of what that test could reach. If a dynamically introduced implementation adds a possible dispatch target relevant to the test, the earlier reachability conclusion may no longer cover all possible paths. SoundSlice could not safely continue relying on that certificate without establishing that the new target cannot affect the test. The mere presence of a new implementation does not, by itself, tell us which individual certificates depend on it.
Does dispatch closure mean a certificate must consider that newly introduced implementation?

Yes, if it is a possible target relevant to the certificate's non-impact claim. Dispatch closure cannot be treated as complete while omitting a target that could make the test reach changed behavior. The question is whether SoundSlice can detect when that possibility changes and invalidate the certificates that no longer justify exclusion.
Could SoundSlice keep a certificate because the implementation was not observed when the test last ran?

Not on that basis alone. An earlier observation cannot rule out a newly possible dispatch target. If the new implementation might change the test's reachability, absence from an earlier run does not certify non-impact. SoundSlice needs a defensible conclusion about the current possibilities before excluding the test.
Does every newly introduced implementation require invalidating every test's certificate?

Not necessarily. The issue is whether the implementation affects the reachability claim made for a particular test. A certificate that can still justify its conclusion despite the new implementation need not be treated as unsound simply because something changed elsewhere. But SoundSlice cannot assume a certificate remains valid where it has not accounted for a potentially relevant new target.
So invalidation is about the certificate's dependencies, not just noticing that a classloader did something?

Exactly. Noticing an introduction is only part of the problem. SoundSlice must determine whether that introduction undermines the dispatch closure or other assumptions supporting a specific exclusion. If it cannot make that determination, it cannot safely rely on the certificate to omit a potentially affected test.
What if the new implementation could be a dispatch target, but the test still passes?

Passing does not establish that the test was unaffected or that the exclusion certificate remains sound. The certificate concerns possible reachability, not a prediction of whether the test will fail. If the implementation leaves open a path to changed behavior, that possibility must be accounted for even when an observed execution passes.
Would invalidating a certificate mean we have proved the test is affected?

No. It means the certificate can no longer justify excluding that test. The test might or might not actually be affected, but an unsupported non-impact claim cannot be used as the basis for omission. That distinction is important: invalidation preserves caution without pretending to know the test's outcome.
Can a certificate be retained if its dispatch closure already covers the introduced implementation?

In principle, yes, if the certificate's justification genuinely covers that implementation and still rules out impact on that test. The question does not establish whether SoundSlice's certificates do so in any particular case. A certificate cannot be retained merely because it is labeled dispatch-closed; its conclusion must remain justified after the possible implementation is considered.
What if SoundSlice cannot determine whether the implementation belongs in a particular test's dispatch closure?

Then uncertainty cannot be used to justify excluding that test. SoundSlice would need to retain any tests that might be affected unless it can establish a safe exclusion. Its proposed full-suite fallback also applies if reflection, generators, or missing dependencies leave relevant impact unresolved. The question does not provide a more specific selection rule for every uncertain classloader introduction.
Does the classloader-backed part of SoundSlice guarantee it will recognize every dynamically introduced implementation?

No guarantee follows from the proposal's name or its use of classloader information. The question specifically asks whether SoundSlice can invalidate certificates when implementations are introduced dynamically. That capability and its completeness would need to be established rather than presumed.
Would it be enough to invalidate certificates for tests that previously executed the new implementation?

That would not necessarily cover tests that could reach it but did not do so in an earlier observed execution. A sound invalidation decision has to respect possible reachability, including relevant dispatch alternatives. The question does not specify a particular rule for identifying affected certificates, so restricting invalidation to observed executions would require justification.
Could an introduction change the validity of a certificate without changing a test's last recorded execution path?

Yes, conceptually. The certificate's claim concerns what the test might reach, not only what it reached previously. An additional possible implementation can matter to that claim even if a past execution path remains unchanged. Whether it matters to a particular certificate depends on the reachability reasoning that supports that certificate.
Why does the 40% threshold become harder to meet when certificates are invalidated?

If SoundSlice cannot use a certificate to exclude a test, that test may have to remain in the selection. More invalidated certificates could therefore increase selection. But invalidation frequency alone would not determine the mean: the selected fractions across all 100 RevisionBench-100 revisions, including any full-suite selections, determine whether the mean exceeds 40%.
Can I avoid invalidation to preserve a smaller selection if the new implementation seems unlikely to run?

No. Low likelihood is not a certificate of non-impact. If the new implementation remains a possible relevant dispatch target, keeping an exclusion solely to protect the 40% mean would sacrifice the safety condition. The efficiency goal has to be met through justified exclusions, not by ignoring a change to the certificate's premises.
Does the question require SoundSlice to select no more than 40% of tests on each revision?

No. It asks about *mean* selection on RevisionBench-100. Individual revisions could select more than 40%, including the full suite when a stated fallback applies. All selections would have to be included in the mean; a low rate on selected revisions alone would not answer the question.
If the mean is exactly 40%, is that considered exceeding 40%?

No. Exactly 40% does not exceed 40%. The numerical part asks whether the mean can stay at or below that value while certificate invalidation remains sound. It supplies no measured mean for SoundSlice.
Could SoundSlice invalidate certificates correctly but still average above 40%?

Yes. Correct invalidation could preserve potentially affected tests while making the selections too large for the mean-selection target. Safety and efficiency are separate requirements. The possibility of an above-target mean is not a reason to reuse a certificate that no longer justifies exclusion.
Could it average below 40% while failing to invalidate a certificate that should be invalidated?

Yes. A low mean would not establish that the selections were safe. If a certificate wrongly excludes a test that might be affected through a dynamically introduced implementation, the invalidation requirement is not met even if the percentage looks favorable.
Would matching full-suite failure detection settle whether invalidation was correct?

Not by itself. A potentially affected test can pass, so a failure-detection match does not validate every certificate or prove that every introduction was accounted for. Full-suite comparison is important for observed failures, while the soundness of exclusions still depends on the reachability justification and appropriate invalidation.
What would it mean to assess the mean fairly if some certificates can no longer be used?

Measure SoundSlice's actual selected-test fraction for each of the 100 revisions with invalidation applied. Include tests retained because certificates are no longer justified and count any full-suite selection as 100% for its revision. Averaging only revisions where certificates remain available would conceal the selection cost at issue.
Does the question say how frequently classloaders introduce implementations on RevisionBench-100?

No. It gives no frequency, no number of affected certificates, and no per-revision selections. We cannot infer whether proper invalidation will keep mean selection at or below 40% or push it above the threshold.
Can we assume a newly introduced implementation is relevant to reflection or generated code?

No. The question concerns classloaders dynamically introducing implementations and their effect on per-test reachability certificates with dispatch closure. Reflection, generators, and missing dependencies remain named fallback conditions in SoundSlice's proposal, but this question does not attribute any particular introduction to one of them.
Does a full-suite fallback prove which certificates were invalidated?

No. Full-suite selection avoids exclusions when the stated uncertainty calls for it; it does not identify every individual certificate that would otherwise be invalid or prove that an introduced implementation affects a particular test. The certificate-invalidation question and the selection outcome should remain distinct.
How should I keep this framed as a question rather than a claim that SoundSlice already works?

Ask whether SoundSlice can detect dynamically introduced implementations, invalidate any per-test reachability certificates whose dispatch closure no longer supports exclusion, and still average at most 40% test selection on RevisionBench-100. That preserves the safety and numerical conditions without asserting an invalidation mechanism or benchmark result.

Here is my hypothesis for SoundSlice: fingerprinting classloader hierarchies and loaded implementation sets will invalidate stale per-test certificates, preserving failure recall at no more than 40% mean test selection. Does that answer the question about dynamically introduced implementations?

It offers a testable answer, not an established result. The predicted mechanism is that fingerprints of both classloader hierarchies and loaded implementation sets will reveal changes that make a per-test reachability certificate stale. SoundSlice would then stop using that certificate to justify excluding a test. The hypothesis also predicts that this conservative invalidation will preserve failure recall while keeping mean test selection at or below 40% on RevisionBench-100.
Why fingerprint both the classloader hierarchy and the set of loaded implementations?

They describe different aspects of the reachability picture. The hierarchy concerns the classloader arrangement relevant to what code a test could reach; the loaded implementation set concerns which implementations are present for dispatch reasoning. A certificate could depend on either. Fingerprinting both is the hypothesis’s proposed way to notice when the basis for a certificate may have changed. It does not, by itself, prove that every relevant change has been captured.
If the loaded implementation set changes, does the hypothesis say every certificate becomes invalid?

No. The prediction concerns *stale* certificates: ones whose exclusion conclusions no longer have a sound basis after the relevant classloader or implementation change. A changed fingerprint calls for reassessing the certificates that might depend on it; the hypothesis does not say every test’s certificate necessarily becomes unsound. Nor does an unchanged-looking certificate remain valid merely because invalidating it would increase selection.
What makes a per-test certificate stale in this context?

A certificate is stale if its claim that a particular test cannot reach affected behavior relies on an account of classloaders or dispatch possibilities that is no longer adequate. A dynamically introduced implementation might add a relevant possible target. If that possibility is missing from the certificate’s dispatch closure, the certificate cannot still justify excluding the test. The hypothesis proposes fingerprints as a way to identify when that risk requires invalidation.
Does invalidating a certificate mean SoundSlice has established that the test will fail?

No. Invalidation means the certificate no longer supports *excluding* that test. The test may pass, fail, or be unaffected; none of those outcomes follows from invalidation alone. The cautious consequence is that SoundSlice cannot omit it on the strength of that stale certificate.
Could a certificate still be valid if a new implementation has loaded?

Possibly, if its reachability argument demonstrably accounts for the new implementation or shows that the new implementation cannot affect that test. The hypothesis does not assume that every load changes every test’s reachability. It does require that certificates whose premises no longer hold be invalidated rather than reused without justification.
What if a hierarchy fingerprint changes but the loaded implementation set appears unchanged?

That is exactly why the hypothesis names the hierarchy separately. A change in the hierarchy may matter to how an existing implementation can be reached, even if the listed implementations have not changed. Whether it affects a particular certificate still needs to be determined; an unchanged implementation set alone would not justify ignoring a potentially relevant hierarchy change.
And if the implementation set changes but the hierarchy does not?

The certificate may need reassessment for a different reason: a newly loaded implementation could add a possible dispatch target under an otherwise unchanged hierarchy. The two fingerprints are intended to reveal distinct changes relevant to dispatch closure. Neither fingerprint, considered in isolation, automatically establishes which tests may be excluded.
Is fingerprint equality proof that a certificate remains valid?

Not without establishing what the fingerprints cover and how that coverage relates to the certificate’s premises. Equality is useful only if relevant classloader and implementation changes could not escape the fingerprinted information. This hypothesis proposes fingerprinting as an invalidation mechanism; it does not specify a fingerprint construction or prove that equality certifies every reachability conclusion.
Does recording loaded implementations establish that no other implementation could later be introduced?

No. A record of what is loaded cannot, merely by existing, rule out a later introduction. If a later implementation could invalidate an exclusion, SoundSlice has to account for that possibility rather than treat an earlier fingerprint as permanent proof. The hypothesis predicts that changes in the relevant fingerprints will invalidate stale certificates; whether the information is complete enough to do so safely remains a substantive question.
Would it be fair to say the fingerprint is an input to certificate validity, not the certificate itself?

Yes. The fingerprint provides information about conditions on which the reachability argument may depend. A per-test certificate still has to justify that the test cannot be affected, including the relevant dispatch closure. Detecting a changed condition can prompt invalidation; a fingerprint alone does not replace the reachability proof.
If a certificate is invalidated, must SoundSlice immediately run the full suite?

Invalidation alone means that certificate can no longer justify omitting its test. The hypothesis does not specify that every invalidated certificate triggers a full-suite run. SoundSlice still has to make a safe selection: it cannot exclude a potentially affected test without valid justification, and its proposed full-suite fallback remains relevant when reflection, generators, or missing dependencies leave impact unresolved. Do not conflate certificate invalidation with a claim that every such event necessarily invokes that fallback.
Could SoundSlice keep an invalidated certificate in use just until the next benchmark run, to avoid selecting too many tests?

That would defeat the predicted safety mechanism. Once a certificate is stale, it cannot justify excluding its test merely because retaining that exclusion helps meet the 40% target. The hypothesis depends on invalidating certificates when their supporting classloader or implementation information no longer suffices.
What exactly does “preserving failure recall” predict?

It predicts that invalidating stale certificates will not sacrifice the failures detectable by the full-suite comparison: the selected tests should retain failure detection rather than omit a test whose failure the full suite would find. It is a prediction about observed detection, not a guarantee that every test which could be affected will necessarily fail or that failure recall alone proves all certificates sound.
Could failure recall look intact even if an affected but passing test was wrongly excluded?

Yes. An affected test may pass, so a failure-detection comparison would not reveal every unsound exclusion. The fingerprint and certificate-validity argument still matters independently of measured failure recall. The hypothesis should not be interpreted as granting permission to exclude a test whenever no missed failure is observed.
Does the 40% limit apply to every RevisionBench-100 revision?

No. The hypothesis says *mean* selection at or below 40%, not a 40% maximum on each revision. Individual selections may be larger. The mean must reflect the tests SoundSlice actually selects after certificate invalidation, including any full-suite selections.
What if the calculated mean is exactly 40%?

Exactly 40% satisfies the stated “at most 40%” prediction. A mean above 40% would not, even if failure recall were preserved. Conversely, a mean below 40% would not establish the prediction if stale certificates were improperly retained or full-suite failures were missed.
Could we measure mean selection using only revisions where certificates remained valid?

That would omit the cost of invalidation and would not test the hypothesis’s mean-selection claim on RevisionBench-100. Selections after invalidating stale certificates, as well as any necessary full-suite selections, must be included. Otherwise the percentage would describe only a favorable subset of revisions.
Does the hypothesis give a maximum number of certificates that can be invalidated?

No. It gives no invalidation count, number of dynamically introduced implementations, or per-revision selection rates. It predicts that SoundSlice will invalidate stale certificates while preserving failure recall at no more than 40% mean selection. The numerical feasibility of that combination cannot be inferred from the proposal alone.
Would detecting a fingerprint change be sufficient evidence that SoundSlice invalidated the right certificates?

No. Detecting a change and applying it correctly to per-test certificate validity are different obligations. To support the hypothesis, SoundSlice must cease relying on certificates made stale by relevant hierarchy or implementation changes, without assuming an unrelated change invalidates or validates a particular test’s reachability claim. The hypothesis does not provide the detailed dependency mapping needed to establish that outcome in advance.
Does this fingerprinting hypothesis make reflection, generated code, and missing dependencies irrelevant?

No. It focuses on invalidating certificates when classloader hierarchies or loaded implementation sets change. SoundSlice’s conservative treatment of unresolved reflection, generators, and missing dependencies remains part of its proposed selection behavior. A valid fingerprint for one aspect of dispatch does not certify exclusions against a different unresolved route to impact.
Is it accurate to describe this as a completed improvement to SoundSlice?

No. This node is a hypothesis about what fingerprinting will accomplish. It reports neither an implemented invalidation mechanism nor observed failure recall or mean selection. Keep the expected behavior and numerical threshold in predictive language.
Can you state it in one precise sentence without turning the prediction into a benchmark result?

Hypothesis: fingerprinting classloader hierarchies and loaded implementation sets will allow SoundSlice to invalidate stale per-test reachability certificates, preserving failure recall while keeping mean test selection on RevisionBench-100 at or below 40%.

Let’s replay RevisionBench-100 with dynamically injected implementations and compare SoundSlice’s certificate invalidation, mean test selection, and failure recall against the full suites. How should I describe the activity?

Replay RevisionBench-100 with implementations introduced dynamically. For each revision, examine whether SoundSlice invalidates per-test reachability certificates whose supporting classloader or dispatch assumptions no longer hold, record the tests it selects, and compare failures detected by that selection with the corresponding full-suite results. Across the 100 revisions, calculate mean selected-test fraction. This specifies what to evaluate, not what the replay will find.
Why compare certificate invalidation as well as selection and failure recall?

They answer different questions. Invalidation concerns whether SoundSlice continues to rely on a certificate after a dynamically introduced implementation makes its reachability claim potentially stale. Selection measures how many tests SoundSlice runs after making those decisions. Failure recall compares the failures those selections detect with failures found by the full suites. A favorable number on one measure does not establish the others.
Should I assume every injected implementation invalidates every test’s certificate?

No. An implementation matters to a particular certificate if it changes a possibility on which that certificate’s exclusion claim depends. The replay should distinguish certificates that need invalidation from ones whose non-impact conclusions remain justified. Neither blanket invalidation nor blanket retention follows merely from saying implementations were injected.
What is the danger if SoundSlice keeps a stale certificate?

It could exclude a test using a reachability argument that no longer accounts for a relevant possible dispatch target. Whether that test actually fails is a separate question. The safety concern is that the certificate might no longer justify ruling out impact, so retaining it solely to keep selection small would be unsound.
Does invalidating a certificate establish that its test is affected?

No. Invalidation withdraws a justification for excluding the test; it does not prove that the test is affected or will fail. SoundSlice may need to select it because potential impact has not been definitively ruled out. The replay should not turn an invalidation event into a claim about a test’s observed outcome.
How would a loaded implementation set matter to this comparison?

A dynamically injected implementation can alter the possible targets relevant to dispatch closure. The certificate-invalidation comparison asks whether SoundSlice accounts for that change where its per-test reachability conclusion depends on the set of possible implementations. The activity does not specify which implementations are injected or how many certificates each one affects.
Does the activity require a particular injection mechanism or a particular kind of implementation?

No. It specifies a replay of RevisionBench-100 with dynamically injected implementations. It does not name a loading procedure, a number of injections, or particular implementations. Those details should not be added to the work description as established facts.
If the classloader hierarchy appears unchanged but a new implementation is introduced, can we treat existing certificates as valid?

Not on that observation alone. A new implementation could affect dispatch closure even without a relevant change to the hierarchy. The question for each certificate is whether its exclusion argument still accounts for the introduced implementation. The replay is intended to examine that behavior rather than assume the answer.
And if the hierarchy changes but the implementation set seems unchanged?

That also calls for assessing whether a certificate’s reachability assumptions remain justified. An apparently unchanged implementation set does not, by itself, establish that a hierarchy change cannot matter.
